questions.question: A 9-year-old girl with psychological problems was started on amitriptyline and then developed dizziness, which had gone by the time she was admitted. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Tricyclics cause orthostatic hypotension and anticholinergic effects (dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention), especially when starting. Review the dose and do an ECG for QTc.

questions.question: Which statement about infantile spasms is NOT correct?
questions.exp: West syndrome = spasms, hypsarrhythmia and regression, peaking at 3–8 months. Causes include tuberous sclerosis, HIE and untreated PKU. First-line treatment is prednisolone/ACTH, or vigabatrin in TSC.
questions.a: They are part of West syndrome
questions.c: They cannot be treated with steroids
questions.d: They are a feature of untreated PKU

questions.question: An 8-month-old has a high sagittal ridge. Head circumference has fallen from the 40th centile at birth to the 3rd. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Premature sagittal suture fusion gives a palpable ridge and a long narrow head (scaphocephaly); head growth may fall across centiles. Confirm with skull X-ray or CT and refer to craniofacial surgery.

questions.question: Which mineral deficiency causes an eczema-like rash and diarrhoea?
questions.exp: Zinc deficiency (acrodermatitis enteropathica): periorificial and acral dermatitis, diarrhoea, alopecia and poor growth.

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy is the shortest in his class with normal examination and delayed bone age. He has stopped going out and refuses to go to school. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Normal examination with delayed bone age fits constitutional delay; the social withdrawal reflects distress about being small, which is common and should be addressed.
questions.c: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

questions.question: A well child has visible haematuria during a URTI that started 3 days ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Synpharyngitic haematuria (within 1–2 days of a URTI) = IgA nephropathy. Post-streptococcal GN appears 1–3 weeks after the throat infection.

questions.question: A 12-year-old's mother died 3 months ago. He is always afraid of dying, and his father is also depressed. What is the best management?
questions.exp: Grief affecting both child and surviving parent is best helped by family-based bereavement support; refer to CAMHS if it becomes prolonged or complicated.
questions.a: Refer to social and mental health services for the child alone
questions.b: Bereavement support for the whole family

questions.question: A child has periorbital oedema and redness with painless, full eye movements and normal vision. What is the best management?
questions.exp: Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis without proptosis, pain on movement or visual change can be treated with oral co-amoxiclav and close review (younger infants or unwell children need IV).

questions.question: A child has had 2 E. coli UTIs. Ultrasound and DMSA are normal. What is the next step?
questions.exp: NICE: recurrent lower UTIs with normal imaging need no further follow-up; advise on hydration, constipation and prompt urine testing with fever.

questions.question: An 8-year-old with cerebral palsy: which finding should make you suspect non-accidental injury?
questions.exp: Bruising on protected sites (upper arms, inner thighs, ears, neck, trunk), patterned bruises and bruises in non-mobile children raise concern. Disabled children are at higher risk of abuse.

questions.question: A 7-month-old has a bruised arm and a fractured humerus. The mother says he fell. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.exp: A humeral shaft fracture in a non-ambulant infant with an inconsistent history is highly suspicious; start a child-protection assessment with skeletal survey.

questions.question: Children with type 1 diabetes are screened regularly for which condition?
questions.exp: NICE: annual thyroid function, coeliac screening at diagnosis and when symptomatic, urine albumin:creatinine ratio from age 12, BP, and retinal screening from 12.

questions.question: A 4-year-old has rapid deep (sighing) breathing and a high blood glucose. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Kussmaul breathing with hyperglycaemia is DKA; check ketones and blood gas.

questions.question: A 10-month-old exclusively breastfed until 6 months has gained 1 kg in the last 3 months. Examination is normal. What do you do?
questions.exp: Weight gain of about 300–400 g/month at 9–12 months is normal; plot on the chart and reassure if following centiles.

questions.question: Which drug is LEAST likely to cause agranulocytosis?
questions.exp: Agranulocytosis is a known risk with carbimazole, clozapine, sulfasalazine, co-trimoxazole and some anticonvulsants (carbamazepine). Topiramate is not associated.

questions.question: A 13-year-old treated for craniopharyngioma 3 years ago has delayed puberty and short stature. What is the most likely reason?
questions.exp: Cranial radiotherapy and the tumour location cause GH and gonadotrophin deficiency. Check pituitary function.
questions.d: Related to the initial disease only

questions.question: A 2-day-old girl rooming-in on the postnatal ward has blue lips around the mouth only; she is otherwise well with normal saturations. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Circumoral (perioral) blueness and acrocyanosis are common and benign in newborns. Central cyanosis of the tongue or low saturations need urgent assessment.

questions.question: What is the best test for gastro-oesophageal reflux disease in children?
questions.exp: Multichannel intraluminal impedance with pH monitoring detects acid and non-acid reflux and correlates with symptoms. Endoscopy looks for oesophagitis or EoE.

questions.question: When is cleft lip usually repaired?
questions.exp: UK practice: cleft lip repair at about 3 months, cleft palate at 6–12 months (before speech develops). Some units repair the lip earlier.

questions.question: A child has moderate to severe stridor, cough and respiratory distress. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Moderate–severe croup: dexamethasone 0.15–0.6 mg/kg and nebulised adrenaline; call senior/anaesthetics if severe with signs of exhaustion.
questions.d: Give steroid (oral dexamethasone) and nebulised adrenaline

questions.question: A brain-dead child is on mechanical ventilation. The family asks that support is not removed. Which ethical principle are they not considering?
questions.exp: Continuing ventilation after brain death has no benefit for the child and uses scarce intensive care resources other children need: distributive justice.

questions.question: A 3-year-old has a rash on the face, mouth, palms and soles. What is the causative agent?
questions.exp: Hand, foot and mouth disease: coxsackie A16 or enterovirus 71, with oral ulcers and vesicles on hands, feet and buttocks.

questions.question: A 13-year-old boy with recurrent abdominal pain and raised faecal calprotectin develops two ecchymotic patches on the back. What is the next investigation?
questions.exp: Probable IBD with bruising suggests vitamin K malabsorption or coagulopathy; check PT/APTT and platelets.

questions.question: Which statement about ostium primum ASD is correct?
questions.exp: Primum ASD is a partial AVSD at the lower septum with a cleft mitral valve; ECG shows left axis deviation. Secundum defects are central.
questions.a: It gives a left-to-right shunt and is associated with mitral regurgitation (cleft mitral valve)
questions.c: It lies in the central part of the septum

questions.question: A female newborn has clitoromegaly, potassium 6.9 mmol/L and low sodium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Virilised 46,XX infant with salt wasting = classic CAH. Check 17-OHP; treat with hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone and salt.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy with autism has banged his head against the wall for 3 months and refuses to wear a hat even in cold weather. What is the best investigation?
questions.exp: A new self-injurious behaviour focused on the head in a non-verbal child can signal pain (headache, raised ICP, dental or ear pain). Look for organic causes; MRI if neurological concern. The recall was uncertain between MRI and TFT.

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy has headache, poor vision, polyuria and short stature. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Craniopharyngioma: headache, bitemporal hemianopia, growth failure and diabetes insipidus; calcified suprasellar mass on imaging.

questions.question: A child has painless haematuria, normal BP and normal examination. Which investigation is most useful?
questions.exp: Idiopathic hypercalciuria is a common cause of isolated haematuria; check urine Ca:Cr ratio along with urine microscopy, renal function and family history.

questions.question: A girl with separated parents and incomplete vaccinations has fever, suprapubic pain, and urine with blood, protein, white cells and positive nitrite. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Suprapubic pain, fever and nitrite-positive pyuria with haematuria indicate bacterial cystitis. Consider safeguarding if the history suggests it.

questions.question: What is the typical EEG in infantile spasms?
questions.exp: Hypsarrhythmia: chaotic high-voltage slow waves with multifocal spikes. 3 Hz spike-wave is childhood absence epilepsy; centrotemporal spikes are benign rolandic epilepsy.

questions.question: A 10-year-old girl without asthma has recurrent chest infections needing repeated antibiotics. Which test is best for diagnosis?
questions.exp: HRCT shows bronchiectasis and its pattern; then look for the cause (CF sweat test, immunoglobulins, ciliary studies).

questions.question: Atrioventricular septal defect is most common in which syndrome?
questions.exp: About 40% of children with Down syndrome have CHD, and AVSD is the most typical lesion.

questions.question: Which statement about puberty is true?
questions.exp: McCune–Albright causes gonadotrophin-independent precocious puberty. Puberty starts with thelarche in girls and testicular volume ≥4 mL in boys; precocity in boys often has a pathological cause.
questions.a: Puberty in girls starts with menarche
questions.c: Precocious puberty in boys is usually idiopathic
questions.d: Testicular volume 2 mL means puberty has started

questions.question: A newborn has IUGR, absent red reflex (cataract), sensorineural hearing loss and a rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Congenital rubella: cataracts, sensorineural deafness, PDA/pulmonary stenosis, 'blueberry muffin' rash and IUGR. CMV causes deafness and periventricular calcification but not cataracts.

questions.question: What is the most common association of meconium aspiration syndrome?
questions.exp: MAS causes airway obstruction, surfactant inactivation and chemical pneumonitis; PPHN is the major complication (treat with oxygen, ventilation, iNO).
questions.d: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

questions.question: What is the most likely cause of seizures in a neonate?
questions.exp: HIE is the commonest cause of neonatal seizures; others are stroke, haemorrhage, infection, hypoglycaemia and hypocalcaemia. The recall only listed metabolic options; between them hyponatraemia is the more plausible cause.

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy plays alongside rather than with other children and lines up his toys. After full history, what do you do?
questions.exp: Possible autism: refer to the multidisciplinary social communication (autism) assessment team and arrange a hearing test.
questions.c: Refer for social communication and developmental assessment

questions.question: A 4-year-old has been eating non-food items (licking surfaces) since 4 months and has brittle hair. Which investigation would help?
questions.exp: Pica suggests iron deficiency and risks lead poisoning; check FBC, ferritin and lead. Brittle hair with neurological signs could also suggest Menkes disease.
questions.c: Blood lead level / full blood count and iron studies

questions.question: A 13-year-old took 30 paracetamol tablets over 12 hours; the last was 2 hours ago. What do you do?
questions.exp: Staggered overdose: the nomogram cannot be used, so start NAC immediately and check level, LFTs, INR and creatinine.
questions.a: Wait for the level and start NAC only if high
questions.c: Give charcoal and send a level
questions.d: Start N-acetylcysteine and send a paracetamol level

questions.question: A 3-year-old has chickenpox with oral lesions and fever. When can he return to nursery?
questions.exp: Varicella is infectious from 2 days before the rash until all lesions have crusted over.
questions.d: When all lesions have crusted (about 5 days after the rash)

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl feels creatures crawling on her skin and has behavioural change; neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: New psychiatric symptoms (hallucinations, behaviour change) in a young child suggest autoimmune (e.g. anti-NMDA receptor) encephalitis; check CSF and serum antibodies. The recall answer was uncertain.

questions.question: A 3-day-old neonate has vomiting and irritability. Blood gas: pH 7.50, bicarbonate 32. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Metabolic alkalosis with vomiting suggests gastric acid loss (pyloric stenosis typically 2–8 weeks). Sepsis, IEM and CAH usually cause acidosis. Urea cycle defects give respiratory alkalosis.

questions.question: A 5-year-old fell off his bicycle. He has amnesia for 10 minutes after the event, has vomited four times and has a parietal haematoma. What do you do?
questions.exp: NICE: three or more episodes of vomiting is an indication for CT head within 1 hour in children.

questions.question: How is congenital CMV infection diagnosed?
questions.exp: Detection of CMV in urine or saliva before 3 weeks confirms congenital infection; after that it may be postnatal. Treat symptomatic babies with valganciclovir.
questions.b: Urine (or saliva) CMV PCR within the first 21 days of life

questions.question: A 4-year-old has fever and red skin, and the skin in the cubital fossa peels off easily. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: SSSS: exfoliative toxin from S. aureus, tender erythroderma with flexural accentuation, positive Nikolsky sign, no mucosal involvement. Treat with IV flucloxacillin.

questions.question: A child treated for constipation for 3 weeks returns with abdominal pain, haematuria and a right-sided abdominal mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: A flank mass with haematuria in a young child is Wilms tumour until proven otherwise; ultrasound then CT/MRI, and avoid repeated palpation.

questions.question: A child has cola-coloured urine after tonsillitis and no skin infection. Which investigation is most likely positive?
questions.exp: After pharyngitis ASO is raised in most; anti-DNase B is better after skin infection. PSGN gives low C3 with normal C4.

questions.question: A neonate with respiratory distress is saturating 94% on a non-rebreathing mask. Which finding is an indication for intubation?
questions.exp: Indications: rising PCO2 above 60–65 mmHg with pH below 7.25, refractory hypoxaemia, apnoea or exhaustion. The recall wrote PCO2 > 50.
questions.a: PCO2 above 60 mmHg (8 kPa) with acidosis

questions.question: Which statement about G6PD deficiency is true?
questions.exp: X-linked; oxidant stress causes acute intravascular haemolysis with jaundice, dark urine, bite cells and Heinz bodies. Neonatal jaundice is common.

questions.question: A child with a UTI treated with trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole develops jaundice. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Sulfonamides are oxidant drugs that precipitate haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of septic arthritis in children over 2 months old?
questions.exp: S. aureus is the commonest overall; Kingella kingae is important in 6 months–4 years; Hib is rare after vaccination; GBS in neonates.

questions.question: A 7-year-old cannot retract his foreskin and has a white scarred ring at the tip. What is the management?
questions.exp: A white scarred ring suggests balanitis xerotica obliterans (lichen sclerosus), which is a true indication for circumcision; topical steroid can be tried. Physiological phimosis without scarring only needs reassurance.
questions.c: Topical steroid; refer for circumcision if it fails or for BXO

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl with operated cleft palate has recurrent ear and chest infections. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cleft palate with recurrent infection (T-cell defect) suggests 22q11 deletion; check calcium, echo and FISH/microarray.

questions.question: An 8-month-old boy has a buttock abscess growing S. aureus and enlarged cervical nodes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Recurrent catalase-positive abscesses with lymphadenitis suggest CGD; do the DHR test.

questions.question: A child has a heliotrope rash and proximal weakness (difficulty climbing stairs and combing hair). Which investigation confirms the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Juvenile dermatomyositis is clinical plus enzymes and MRI; muscle biopsy is the gold standard when needed. (Recall had two questions on JDM.)

questions.question: A 6-week-old boy has two rib fractures that the radiologist dates at about 6 weeks old. The mother says labour was difficult. What do you do?
questions.exp: Rib fractures from birth are rare (big babies, shoulder dystocia). Any infant rib fracture needs a skeletal survey, coagulation and bone tests and safeguarding review.
questions.c: It is mostly birth trauma; give analgesia and follow up
questions.d: It could be birth trauma, but NAI must be excluded: full child-protection work-up

questions.question: A 13-year-old girl has not had menarche. She is short, SMR 2–3. Her mother had menarche at 16 and her sister at 15. Bone age is 11.5 years. What do you do?
questions.exp: Puberty has started, bone age is delayed and there is a family history of late menarche: constitutional delay. Primary amenorrhoea is investigated at 15 (or 3 years after thelarche).
questions.b: Reassure and follow up in 6 months

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl has a small face and chin, a murmur, neonatal jaundice and follow-up with a nephrologist. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Alagille (JAG1): bile duct paucity with cholestasis, peripheral pulmonary stenosis, butterfly vertebrae, posterior embryotoxon, triangular face and renal anomalies.

questions.question: A 24-hour-old baby with features of Down syndrome has a murmur. You cannot see the red reflex because he moves, and there is mild abdominal distension during feeds. What do you do?
questions.exp: Down syndrome: all babies need an echo; a murmur needs review before discharge. Absent red reflex needs ophthalmology review within 2 weeks (cataract). Watch for duodenal atresia/Hirschsprung.
questions.a: Arrange an echo and senior review before discharge, and refer to ophthalmology

questions.question: A family arrived from Africa 4 days ago. A 5-year-old boy has haematuria. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Urinary schistosomiasis causes terminal haematuria; diagnose with eggs in terminal urine (midday) and treat with praziquantel. (Arrival 4 days ago means infection was earlier.)

questions.question: An infant has episodes of back arching and abnormal movements during or an hour after feeds; they cannot be soothed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Sandifer syndrome: paroxysmal dystonic posturing (neck/back arching) related to gastro-oesophageal reflux, often mistaken for seizures.

questions.question: A 13-year-old boy has weakness of the right arm and left leg; neurological examination is normal. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: A non-anatomical pattern (crossed arm/leg) with normal signs suggests a functional disorder; confirm with positive signs (e.g. Hoover sign).

questions.question: A child has epistaxis; his mother has menorrhagia. Bleeding time is prolonged. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Mucocutaneous bleeding with prolonged bleeding time and an affected mother (autosomal dominant) suggests vWD; APTT may be normal or mildly prolonged.

questions.question: What is the first management step in DKA?
questions.exp: BSPED: start fluids first, and begin insulin (no bolus) 1–2 hours after IV fluids to reduce cerebral oedema risk.
questions.b: IV 0.9% saline alone, with insulin infusion started 1–2 hours later
questions.d: IV saline and insulin infusion together

questions.question: A 4-year-old has a swollen painful knee, fever and cannot bear weight. What do you do?
questions.exp: Suspected septic arthritis: aspirate (culture before antibiotics when possible), then IV antibiotics; washout if pus.
